paragraphs.heading: Matter we cannot see
paragraphs.text: Dark matter is an unseen, hypothetical kind of matter that does not interact with light or any other electromagnetic radiation. Astronomers infer it from gravity: some effects cannot be explained by general relativity unless there is more matter than we can observe. Apart from gravity, it is not known to interact with ordinary matter or radiation. That makes it hard to detect in a laboratory.

paragraphs.heading: How much there is
paragraphs.text: In the standard Lambda-CDM model of cosmology, the universe's mass and energy is 68.2% dark energy, 26.8% dark matter and 5% ordinary matter. That makes dark matter 85% of all the mass. It is dense in the halo around a galaxy but thin in our Solar System. All the dark matter out to Neptune's orbit would add up to about 10¹⁷ kg, roughly the mass of one large asteroid.

paragraphs.heading: Scaffolding for galaxies
paragraphs.text: Dark matter is thought to act as a gravitational scaffold for structures in the universe. After the Big Bang, it collected into blobs strung along thin filaments, and superclusters of galaxies built up into a cosmic web. Its pull shows up in how galaxies form and in how galaxies move inside galaxy clusters.

paragraphs.heading: Zwicky and the Coma Cluster
paragraphs.text: Galaxy clusters gave an early clue. In 1933 Fritz Zwicky estimated the mass of the Coma Cluster in two ways: from the motions of galaxies near its edge, and from its brightness and number of galaxies. The first estimate was about 400 times the second. The visible galaxies had far too little gravity for such fast orbits, so Zwicky concluded that unseen matter, which he called dunkle Materie, was holding the cluster together.

paragraphs.heading: Right idea, wrong numbers
paragraphs.text: Zwicky's figures were off by more than a factor of ten, mainly because he used an outdated value of the Hubble constant. Even so, he correctly concluded that most of the matter pulling on the cluster was dark. Unlike today's theories, though, he thought of it as ordinary matter that simply gave off no light.

paragraphs.heading: Halos around galaxies
paragraphs.text: The idea really took hold in the 1970s, when several kinds of observation were combined to argue that galaxies sit inside halos of unseen matter. In 1974 two independent groups, one in Princeton and one in Tartu, Estonia, reached that conclusion. One key piece of evidence was the shape of galaxy rotation curves. Vera Rubin and Kent Ford used a new spectrograph to measure these curves more accurately in spiral galaxies seen edge-on.

paragraphs.heading: What could it be
paragraphs.text: The most popular explanation is a subatomic particle not yet discovered, such as WIMPs or axions. The other main option is that dark matter is made of primordial black holes. A minority of astrophysicists instead propose changing the laws of gravity, with ideas such as MOND. So far, no such theory explains all the evidence at once, which suggests some dark matter would still be needed.
